sentences.text: The genus Aptornis stands alone as the only member of the extinct family Aptornithidae.
This group contains two confirmed species, Aptornis otidiformis and Aptornis defossor, alongside a third provisional species, ?Aptornis proasciarostratus.
These birds measured approximately 80 cm in length and weighed about 18 kg, making them roughly the size of small moa.
They possessed enormous, downward-curving, and pointed bills.
As flightless birds with extremely reduced wings and a uniquely reduced carpometacarpus, their wings were proportionally smaller than those of the dodo.
The common name 'adzebill' refers to the bird's reinforced beak, which resembles a woodworking adze tool.
The Māori name for Aptornis defossor was 'ngutu hahau'.
Biologist Richard Owen first described adzebills scientifically in 1844.
Richard Owen initially mistook adzebills for a small species of moa.
Richard Owen speculated that adzebills were omnivores, a hypothesis supported by stable isotope analysis of their bones, and they became extinct before European explorers arrived in New Zealand.
Adzebill fossils have been found only in the lowland, drier areas of New Zealand.
Adzebills lived from the Miocene epoch through the Holocene and were endemic to New Zealand.
The two known species of adzebill were divided between the North Island and the South Island of New Zealand.
The taxonomic placement of adzebills within the order Aves has been a subject of long-standing debate.
A 2011 genetic study classified Aptornis defossor as a member of the Gruiformes lineage.
Two 2019 studies proposed different close relatives for adzebills: one linked them to flufftails (Sarothruridae) and the other to trumpeters (Psophiidae).
A 2025 study identified Nesotrochis as the sister taxon to the adzebill family.
